Croatia sits on the southeastern edge of Europe, with a long, narrow coastline rather like Chile’s. It is a young country that was going through a brutal war little more than twenty years ago. Many people may not know much about it, but certain groups will immediately think of certain symbols.

Those who follow politics will think of “Yugoslavia” and “Tito.”

Football fans can’t get past “the Checkered Ones” and “Modrić.”

Music lovers will surely think of Maksim Mrvica’s “Croatian Rhapsody,” a piece born from the ruins of war.

For Er Mu, a keen traveler and a longtime Game of Thrones fan, the name that leaps to mind is Dubrovnik. This medieval walled city at Croatia’s southern tip was the main filming location for King’s Landing, the seat of power in Westeros.

Long before Game of Thrones aired, this little town, known as the Pearl of the Adriatic, was already a famous resort that drew crowds of visitors every year and was called “Europe’s back garden.” Once the show aired, even more people came on pilgrimage to King’s Landing, Er Mu among them.

Where Queen Cersei met her judgment

The dock where Sansa was sent away

Where the High Sparrow gave his speech

Beyond the white walls lies the famous Blackwater Bay

The dragons’ dungeon

The city walls and the Adriatic

The July weather was glorious and the sky was very blue. Standing on the city walls and gazing into the distance, sea and sky really did merge into one, and the clear sunlight on the white walls made it obvious why the city is called the Pearl of the Adriatic…

Ziyu: Stop, stop, stop! This is a serious popular-acoustics account. Are you turning it into a travel blog?

Er Mu: Wouldn’t be the worst idea. (evil grin)

Look at a map of Croatia and what sticks in your mind is that long, thin coastline. Apart from the capital, Zagreb, all its famous cities lie along it.

Dubrovnik is at the southern end. Heading north you reach Split, Croatia’s second-largest city and the capital of Split-Dalmatia County. Farther north still is the historic city of Zadar, the administrative center of Zadar County and northern Dalmatia. Zadar is home to the Sea Organ (Morske orgulje), one of the world’s three famous organs that play without a player:

During the Second World War and the Croatian War of Independence at the end of the last century, the Zadar region was at the center of the fighting, and the whole city was badly damaged.

At the start of the new century the government launched a huge project to reshape the entire Zadar waterfront, and the Sea Organ was part of it. It was designed by the well-known Croatian architect Nikola Bašić and opened to the public when it was completed in April 2005.

Locals and tourists loved it from the start: while strolling by the sea and watching the stunning Adriatic sunset, you can also listen to the sea play. The following year the giant organ won the European Prize for Urban Public Space.

So how does this giant musical installation make its sound?

The whole Sea Organ is built beneath the waterfront promenade. It is 75 m long and made up of seven sections spaced about 4.5 m apart, which you can tell apart by their different numbers of steps. Each section contains five pipes, about 1.5 m apart.

Each pipe has three main parts:

1. A horizontal rubber pipe below sea level, open to the sea

2. A sounding steel pipe with an opening, directly beneath the promenade

3. A narrower rubber pipe connecting the horizontal pipe to the sounding pipe

Wind, tides and passing ships make the sea level rise and fall. Through the connecting rubber pipes, this pushes the air in the sounding steel pipes back and forth, producing a tone of a particular pitch (frequency) at the opening, somewhere between 60 and 250 Hz. The sound then reaches listeners through outlets in the side of the steps. Broadly speaking, the Sea Organ is a wind instrument, like a flute or a reed pipe. We will explain how wind instruments produce sound in more detail in a future article.

Wind, tides and passing ships are all random, so the movement of the water, the source of excitation (the “player”), is also largely random. Don’t expect it to perform the “Croatian Rhapsody” like Maksim. But it was rebuilt from the very ruins of war that the Rhapsody describes. Beyond offering a fun public space, this experimental piece of musical art may also bring comfort and hope to the people of a city and a country that suffered two brutal wars in modern times.

Video: YouTube

And what would a “travel blog with a science ad slipped in” be without food?

The ice cream here holds its own against the much-loved Italian gelato across the sea. Maybe it’s because both share the same subtropical Mediterranean climate? Summer days are really hot, and you need something to cool you down.
